When someone or something is biased, it means they are unfairly tilted in one direction — leaning toward one side, person, or idea — in a way that makes balanced, fair judgment impossible.

Think of a weighing scale. A fair scale sits perfectly level and weighs things truthfully. A biased scale is secretly tilted — it always tips one way no matter what you place on it. It cannot give you an honest reading because it is already leaning before the weighing even begins.

That "secret tilt" is what biased means.

There are two key ingredients in the word "biased":

1. A preference or prejudice — a person or thing already favors one side, or already dislikes one side, before giving something a fair look.

2. That preference is unfair — it is not based on solid evidence, logic, or reason. It comes from personal feelings, past experiences, cultural conditioning, self-interest, or simply a closed mind.

Without both ingredients, the word doesn't fully apply. Simply having an opinion doesn't make you biased. You become biased when your judgment is distorted by a pre-existing lean that you are unwilling — or unable — to set aside.

"Biased" can lean in either of two directions:

  • Biased in favor of something = unfairly supporting it, giving it too much credit, or seeing it in an unrealistically positive light.
  • Biased against something = unfairly opposing it, dismissing it too quickly, or seeing it in an unrealistically negative light.

Examples:

  • A judge who secretly wants one team to win is biased in favor of that team.
  • A teacher who gives lower grades to students she personally dislikes is biased against them.
  • A news channel that only reports stories that make one political party look bad is biased against that party.
Biased Can Be Conscious or Unconscious

This is a very important nuance.

Sometimes, a biased person knows they are being unfair and does it deliberately. A corrupt referee who has been bribed to make bad calls in a game is consciously biased.

But very often — and this is what makes bias so tricky — a person is biased without even realizing it. Their upbringing, culture, personal experiences, or emotions have quietly shaped how they see the world, and they genuinely believe they are being fair, even when they are not.

For example, a hiring manager might unconsciously prefer candidates who remind him of himself — same background, same university, same way of speaking — without ever noticing this pattern. He feels like he's just "going with his gut," but he is actually biased.

This unconscious form is sometimes called implicit bias, and it is considered particularly important to understand because the person cannot correct a bias they don't know they have.

"Biased" is a very flexible word. It is used to describe:

People — "The journalist is biased; she only interviews people who agree with her."

Sources of information — "That website is biased — it only presents one side of the argument."

Systems and institutions — "The hiring process is biased against women."

Research and data — "The study's results are biased because the sample only included wealthy participants."

Opinions and recommendations — "His review of his own company's product is obviously biased."

Bias is not always all-or-nothing. It exists on a scale:

  • Slightly biased — a small lean, somewhat fair overall
  • Heavily biased / deeply biased / strongly biased — an extreme lean, very unfair
  • Biased toward or biased against — specifying the direction

It's important not to confuse biased with simply having a point of view. Every human being has perspectives, preferences, and opinions — that is completely normal and does not make them biased.

What crosses the line into biased is when a person refuses to consider other information fairly, ignores contradicting evidence, or lets their preference cloud their judgment in a situation that calls for fairness and objectivity.

A scientist who has a hypothesis is not automatically biased — but if she ignores data that disproves her hypothesis just because she wants to be right, she is being biased.
The opposite of biased is unbiased or impartial — meaning fair, balanced, not tilted in any direction. Related words include neutral, objective, and unprejudiced.
Biased means unfairly tilted toward or against something, in a way that prevents honest, balanced judgment — whether the person realizes it or not.
